items.fullDescription: "It is worse, much worse, than you think" states David Wallace-Wells at the opening of his The Uninhabitable Earth: Life After Warming (2019). "When do we start physically attacking the things that consume our planet and destroy them with our own hands?" asks Andreas Malm in How to Blow Up a Pipeline (2021). "I don't think about hope much anymore. But I do think about imagination," writes Terry Tempest Williams in an interview contained in A voice in the Wilderness: Conversations with Terry Tempest Williams (2006). In the spaces between these statements we encounter a range of reactions to our warming condition, from blunt pessimism, to righteous anger, to nuanced reframing. Triangulating these sentiments, we arrive at an undeniable point of ecopessimism, an overwhelming feeling that everything is speeding toward destruction, the painful realization that perhaps Earth, "the only home we've ever known" to quote Carl Sagan, is no longer so welcoming. Counterintuitively, the narrative trope of the looming threat of an "inhospitable earth" may facilitate a denial of the reality of climate crisis. The narrative ubiquity of natural disasters, futures of scarcity, and apocalyptic hellscapes results in a figuring of an Earth incompatible with human life as an easily dispelled bogeyman looming familiarly, and therefore toothlessly, over future climate scenarios. What happens, however, if we read the "end of the world" instead as an ego death of the anthropocene? If the idea of an "inhospitable earth" no longer gains imaginative traction in advocacy or art, then we are tasked with imagining an afterlife for Earth as informed by an ethic of hospitality. The opposite of an "inhospitable earth" is not merely one that is conducive to human survival; being "hospitable" is defined as "affording welcome and entertainment to strangers." How can an ethic of hospitality bend ecopessimism into something worth, as it were, entertaining? If the "end of the world" is certain, what might it look like, as Wendell Berry poetically urges us, to "practice resurrection"? This ASLE affiliated panel welcomes proposals that address the question of how to live (and entertain) in a world on fire. We are especially interested in work that moves beyond abstract hope and optimism to address the complex and overwhelming force of the overlapping crises of our time. If the worst must be assumed, where does that leave us? And what imaginings should we entertain while here? Possible topics may include: -The roles and limits of art and literature in addressing world crises. -Climate realism, doomerism, ecofascism, abundance and other ideologies that address the realities of an inhospitable Earth. -The uses/abuses of hope in understanding and planning for possible inhospitable futures. -The place of imagination in creating more hospitable futures. -Successes/Failures of environmental/climate justice in creating more equitable futures. -The image of technology such as A.I. or space travel as solutions to or escapes from climate collapse. -Treatment of the Other, broadly conceived, in light of environmental/climate crisis. -Any other topic that considers the overbearing presence of climate collapse, open subject area and time period. Please send abstracts of 250-500 words, along with A/V requirements and a brief bio, to Jency Wilson (jwilson17@una.edu) and Matt Spencer (mls0142@auburn.edu) by 24 August 2026.

items.fullDescription: Date: October 10-11, 2026 Location: SMU Main Campus, Dallas, TX Theme: Movement & Borderlands Abstract Submission Deadline: August 28, 2026 Keynotes: Dr. Tim Bowman & Dr. Elda María Román Graduate students of Southern Methodist University's Departments of English, History, and Anthropology, in collaboration with the Moody School of Advanced Studies, Dedman College Interdisciplinary Institute, and the department of English, have collaborated to hold the third annual Engaging Research Across the Humanities (ERAH) Conference at SMU from October 10-October 11, 2026. ERAH 2026 will prioritize the development of interdisciplinary connections and aims to foster a supportive environment for both graduate students and advanced undergraduates engaged in strong research. There will be special emphasis placed on creating opportunities for participants with limited or no prior conference experience. The theme for ERAH 2026 is Movement & Borderlands. If you have any questions, please email arundhatig@smu.edu. Borders simultaneously construct and limit meaning. By demarcating entities, we hold the power to define space and identity. In the same manner, those entities are restricted to oppositional definitions. What does it mean to occupy borderlands, to move across them and through them? How is the deconstruction of borders, or reconceptualization of definitional demarcation, itself an act of meaning-making that exists without opposition? How do borderlands complicate cultural conceptions rooted in duality? How does movement across and through borderlands produce opportunity for new forms of meaning-making not rooted in hard lines and limitations? This year's theme asks us to think critically about the roles of both movement and borderlands in our respective disciplines by considering these questions and others. We invite you to consider the roles of both movement and borderlands within the works you study-be it literary works, historical archives, etc.-as well as how pervasive disciplinary paradigms shape the ways in which you approach your scholarship. Possible topics may include but are not limited to: Migration, mobility, and displacement Citizenship and belonging Racial, ethnic, national, religious identity Borders as constructs Frontiers Artistic and embodied movement Indigenous perspectives on imposed borders Nationalism and borderlands Environmental and ecological borders Linguistic borders Tourism and global circulation We invite abstracts of 200-250 words for both individual presentations and fully-constructed panels (3-4 speakers). items.fullDescription: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems, in contemporary digital society, have drastically evolved from statistical tools to principal instruments of knowledge production, validation and dissemination. Large language models (LLMs), automated search systems, and predictive algorithms increasingly dictate what society knows, how knowledge is validated, and who is recognized as an expert/authority. This shift demands a rigorous critique from the perspective of the sociology of knowledge to evaluate how power, inequality, and social structures are embedded within these automated epistemic tools. The panel invites contributions that explore this socio-epistemic duality of AI through conflicting dynamics: Societal Hospitality and Structural Hostility. This infrastructure relies on the extraction of human cognitive labor, the enclosure of the global intellectual commons, and the automated erasure of marginalized ways of knowing. The back end of AI systems enforces a rigid epistemology that encodes historical social biases, presenting them as neutral, objective, mathematical truths. This panel seeks to bring together scholars, theorists, and empirical researchers to map this friction. The panel aims to explore how AI acts simultaneously as an infrastructure of social integration and a vector of epistemic alienation. items.fullDescription: Conference online (via Zoom) CFP: To remember sometimes means to experience again. That is the case of trauma. However, recovery from trauma is also based on memory. The question, then, is not how to forget painful memories, but how to remember without suffering. During this conference we would like to concentrate on the phenomena of trauma and recovery, to look at how memory is involved in the traumatic experience and the recovery process and explore, among other questions, what we remember and forget, what causes suffering and how to deal with it. We are interested in all aspects of traumatic experiences, in their individual and collective dimensions, in the past and in the present-day world. We would like to examine the role of memory in both falling into trauma and overcoming it. Thus, we want to describe the phenomena of trauma and recovery in their multifarious manifestations: psychological, social, historical, cultural, philosophical, religious, economic, political, and many others. As usual, we also want to devote considerable attention to how these phenomena appear in artistic practices: literature, film, theatre or visual arts. That is why we invite researchers representing various academic disciplines: anthropology, history, psychiatry, psychology, psychoanalysis, sociology, politics, philosophy, economics, law, literary studies, theatre studies, film studies, memory studies, migration studies, consciousness studies, dream studies, gender studies, postcolonial studies, medical sciences, cognitive sciences, and urban studies and others. Different forms of presentations are encouraged, including case studies, theoretical inqueries, problem-oriented arguments or comparative analyses. We will be happy to hear from both experienced scholars and young academics at the start of their careers, as well as doctoral and graduate students. This session aims to foster dialogue across disciplinary and institutional boundaries to move toward shared frameworks for teaching museum ethics that support emerging practitioners in imagining and enacting ethical futures.

items.fullDescription: Pendant la période de l'Indochine française, les premiers vietnamiens sont acheminés en Nouvelle-Calédonie en tant que travailleurs sous-contrat dans les mines de nickel. Cette période marque en parallèle la rébellion très présente des autochtones de l'île - les Kanak - face à la dépossession territoriale des colons français. Le refus de participer à l'industrie minière d'un groupe favorise l'expatriation de l'autre sur l'archipel en pleine ère de la colonisation française dans plusieurs colonies. Le roi tonkinois Ham Nghi, à l'âge de 18 ans, a été placé en exil en Algérie après des années de mouvements de résistance contre la puissance coloniale française. Son expulsion fait écho à celle de la Reine malgache Ranavalona III, qui a eu lieu après l'annexion de Madagascar par la France en 1896. L'ensemble de l'empire français, étendu de l'Indochine à l'Afrique insulaire, est sujet à la déportation dans la plus grande colonie de peuplement. Ce réseau de déportation des colonies liées met en avant la question des outils de domination employés par le système colonial. Malgré les différentes populations colonisées, la stratégie de domination s'applique d'une certaine façon. **** Dans le cadre académique au sein des études francophones et françaises, nous voyons souvent des pistes de spécialisation distinctes, telles que les études européennes, les études caribéennes, et les études postcoloniales francophones. Les cours d'histoire et de littérature offrent également des réflexions particulières selon une région spécifique ainsi qu'une époque donnée. L'objectif de former les futurs chercheurs dans des domaines précis, faute d'études approfondies sur les caractéristiques transcontinentales, risque de faire oublier qu'au coeur de l'histoire de l'un est tissée celle de l'autre. Cette imbrication transnationale et transcommunautaire, inévitable soit-elle, est due à la fois aux déplacements migratoires, à l'exil d'après-guerre, et à la mobilisation de la force de travail par le système capitaliste et colonial. Lorsque l'on met en évidence ce lien intrinsèque entre des événements, on fait émerger un réseau transcolonial qui lie l'Afrique, l'Asie, et/ou l'Europe. Ce réseau nous oblige à réfléchir à l'interconnexion de l'un à l'autre, d'une communauté spécifique à une autre soi-disant éloignée. Dans le contexte du monde d'aujourd'hui, une telle conscience de l'interconnexion des histoires coloniales peut susciter des réflexions : Peut-on vraiment ignorer le combat de l'autre ? Quels seront les enjeux ? Communications à envoyer soit en anglais, soit en français.

items.fullDescription: The Institute of Contemporary History and the Institute of Philosophy of the Czech Academy of Sciences invite proposals for a two-day international conference bringing together historical scholarship and contemporary reflections on civic activism and democratic resistance. Held on the occasion of the fiftieth anniversary of the founding of Charter 77, the conference does not seek merely to commemorate a landmark of Czech and Czechoslovak history. Rather, it aims to reassess Charter 77 as a historically situated yet internationally significant experiment in civic resistance, and to explore its changing meanings in an era marked by democratic backsliding, geopolitical fragmentation, and the transformation of the global human rights order. The conference seeks to foster dialogue across disciplinary, geographical, and generational boundaries between scholars and civic actors concerned with the past, present, and future of democracy and human rights. Charter 77 emerged in 1977, during the normalization period in Czechoslovakia, as a culturally and politically distinctive act of civic resistance "from below" in defense of fundamental human rights. It soon became not merely a symbol but an enduring platform of democratic opposition to late communist dictatorship, whose language, practices, and moral authority resonated far beyond Czechoslovakia. Recent scholarship has highlighted both Charter 77's rootedness in the political and intellectual context of the late Cold War and its lasting significance as a distinctive experiment in civic resistance. Today, when the international order shaped by the Helsinki process is undergoing profound transformation, when global consensus on human rights is increasingly contested, and when democratic institutions face mounting pressure, Charter 77 offers an important historical perspective for rethinking questions of human dignity, civic responsibility, pluralism, and nonviolent resistance. The notion of social imagination , understood as the capacity to envision alternative forms of political and civic life, lies at the heart of this conference. Likewise, the idea of the (post-)global age refers to an increasingly fragmented international landscape in which universal aspirations coexist with renewed geopolitical rivalry, regionalization, and competing visions of democracy, sovereignty, and human rights. The conference will bring together scholars from history, philosophy, political science, legal studies, cultural anthropology, sociology, and related disciplines alongside contemporary civic actors. It aims to explore the intellectual and political legacy of dissent, its transformations after 1989, and the ways in which the Chartist ethos may illuminate current debates on democracy, human rights, civic engagement, and nonviolent resistance. The program will move across three broad, interconnected registers: the historical legacy of Charter 77 itself, situated within Czech/Slovak, Central European, and global frames; the trajectories of contemporary anti-authoritarian and democratizing movements across Eastern Europe (from Serbia and Belarus to Russia and Georgia); and the wider global dimensions of present-day human rights and democratization struggles. Contributions are welcome that speak to any of these registers, or that move between them. We invite proposals addressing, among others, the following themes - though contributions are by no means limited to this list: Charter 77 in comparative perspective: dissidence, opposition, and civic initiatives across socialist Europe. Eastern Europe and international human rights organizations: historical links between dissidence and its contemporary forms. Human rights and the transformation of the international system: the evolution of international norms from Helsinki to the present. Religion, ethics, and human rights in dissident thought. Social imagination and the language of resistance: how concepts of human dignity, solidarity, and civic responsibility continue to shape contemporary activism. Transnational solidarity across political regimes: historical dissident networks and contemporary forms of digital mobilization. Law, institutional independence, and civic oversight: dissident legalism, authoritarian legality, and contemporary legal resistance. The ethics of nonviolence and the limits of civil disobedience: theory and practice across different historical contexts. Cultural opposition and artistic imagination: forms of cultural dissent, past and present, and the question of creative freedom under conditions of digital surveillance and platform capitalism. The memory of dissent in public space: institutionalization, contested narratives, and the relationship between history, politics, and activism. Political order and civil resistance in the age of artificial intelligence: surveillance, disinformation, repression, and democratic resilience in historical perspective. Civic engagement after 1989: continuities, transformations, and forgotten traditions of democratic participation. items.fullDescription: Transatlantic Connections and the 'Special Relationship[s]': BAAS Postgraduate Symposium, 2026 V&A East Storehouse, London 9th November In 1946, Winston Churchill declared the need for a "special relationship between the British Commonwealth and Empire and the United States" in order to maintain world diplomacy, citing our shared language and cultural values as connecting the two countries. Although this 'special relationship' has continually been called into question by scholars, there is undoubtedly a channel of cultural and political exchange between the US and the UK, as well as with other countries, which has become even more urgent for discussion in recent years. The 2026 BAAS Postgraduate Symposium invites proposals from postgraduate researchers at all levels and across all disciplines on the topic of Transatlantic Connections and the 'Special Relationship[s]'. By using the term 'Special Relationship[s]', we intend to explore the relationship between not only the US and the UK, but also between the US and other countries. We invite panels and individual papers on this theme and encourage you to interpret it as broadly as you wish, including any aspect of the US's transnational cultural, political and literary connections, influences or contrasts. We welcome contributions from all realms of American Studies, including, but not limited to: literature and film studies, postcolonial and decolonial analysis, science and visual culture, and urban and environmental history. As this year's symposium will be held at V&A East Storehouse, the site of the David Bowie Archive, we are particularly keen on hearing from scholars exploring the etymologically and culturally rich prefix of the term 'Transatlantic' itself. This one-day symposium will involve not only academic panel discussions, but other activities such as a career development session, an introduction to the archives at the Victoria and Albert Museum, and a keynote address by Professor Mark Ford. The intention is to foster a strong postgraduate community in American Studies and to learn from both our peers and from leaders in our field. The symposium will be catered, hosted primarily in-person at V&A East Storehouse, but with a digital attendance option for those only able to join online. There will be time in the day to explore V&A East Storehouse and the David Bowie Centre. V&A East Storehouse is a working museum store with a rich archive for students to use in their research. The building is designed to allow visitors to get closer to objects held in the V&A collections and to the work of the museum itself. We welcome the submission of individual papers as well as proposals for complete panels of three researchers. Applications from groups of three or four researchers for roundtable discussions are also welcome. For panel and roundtable proposals, please also include a statement of up to 200 words on the aims of the collective submission, alongside the individual papers. Papers should be around 15-20 minutes long , and roundtables will consist of five-minute introductions by each researcher followed by 45 minutes of discussion. Interdisciplinary paper, panel and roundtable proposals are encouraged. Suggested paper and roundtable topics include, but are not limited to: - Case studies or broader comparisons between literary texts from the US and other nations - Case studies or broader comparisons between films from the US and other nations - Comparative political or historical analyses concerning the US and other nations - Comparative economic, scientific or environmental analyses concerning the US and other nations. Although the symposium will centre on 'Transatlantic Connections', we welcome proposals making any transnational comparisons rooted in American Studies. We especially encourage researchers from across Europe and beyond to submit and attend, as part of ongoing efforts to expand the EAAS community of postgraduates. We want to make this symposium as accessible as possible; we will be working to ensure a relaxed academic environment and we encourage anyone attending to email us with any access needs. Bursaries will be available from BAAS on a limited basis for students requiring financial support for attendance. If you have any questions about the symposium, big or small, please get in touch and we will be happy to help. We look forward to hearing from you!

items.fullDescription: American Comparative Literature Association 2027 Annual Meeting University of Houston May 20-23 The Poverty of Literature Organizer: Gabriel Quigley, University of Victoria (gabrielquigley@uvic.ca) How does literature represent poverty? Is poverty available for representation? The title of this seminar is taken from Marx's The Poverty of Philosophy, which, in turn, subverts Proudhon's The Philosophy of Poverty. In it, Marx critiques the approach taken by Proudhon and other anarchist, communist, or socialist "theoreticians" who assume that economic categories exist independently of history. According to Marx, "so long as they look for science and merely make systems, so long as they are at the beginning of the struggle, they see in poverty nothing but poverty, without seeing in it the revolutionary, subversive side, which will overthrow the old society." A similar critique might be leveled at today's writers and critics: when literature and literary criticism engage with poverty at all, do they merely reduce it to an ahistorical economic category? What forms of reification, alienation, and exploitation does the literary assumption that poverty is available for representation produce? This seminar asks what literature owes to people experiencing poverty. At a time when 847 million people live in extreme poverty-95% of whom are in the Global South-it seeks to bring together research on the representation, history, and ontological status of poverty. Unlike Marx's "theoreticians," who "see in poverty nothing but poverty," scholars analyzing poverty through other frameworks-such as ethical demand, affective complexity, geopolitical disparities, aesthetic fetishization, and state failure-are strongly encouraged to submit abstracts. Papers may respond to such questions as: how should poverty be represented, if at all? Beyond an economic category, can poverty be conceived as an aesthetic, metaphysical, or phenomenological category? How is the concept of poverty entangled with conceptions of lack, deprivation, or destitution? How does the global distribution of poverty reflect the ongoing injuries of imperialism, colonialism, neocolonialism, globalization, and ecological catastrophe? Possible topics: - Poverty and realism; poverty and genre - The ethics of speaking for the poor - Testimony, life writing, and first-person accounts of poverty - Poverty and racial capitalism - Postcolonial and decolonial frameworks for poverty - Poverty and ecological catastrophe; climate precarity - Poverty and intersectionality (race, gender, sexuality, disability) - "Poverty porn," sentimentality, and voyeurism - Working-class literature and labor - Poverty in the Global South; imperialism and uneven development - Urban and rural poverty as literary landscapes - Homelessness and houselessness - Poverty and the archive - Poverty and affect: shame, solidarity, rage - The literary canon and class; institutional gatekeeping - Austerity, welfare, and the state in literature - Migration, displacement, and border crossing - Literature and human rights - Poverty as aesthetic, metaphysical, or phenomenological category - Poverty and ontology; being, lack, and deprivation - Bare life and destitution ACLA Seminar Description can be accessed here: https://www.acla.org/seminar/63e1eb87-fe99-49c9-aac0-517ccf904102. items.fullDescription: TITLE: Language Learning Beyond the Classroom: Virtual Exchanges, Platforms, and AI MODALITY: Hybrid: The session will be held in-person but a few remote presentations may be included. CHAIRS: Liana Ewald (Massachusetts Institute of Technology), Dagmar Jaeger (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) ABSTRACT: This session explores the growing role of virtual exchanges, commercial platforms, and AI-mediated interactions in language, literature, and culture courses. In recent years, many instructors have experimented with new ways of connecting students with speakers, authors, and communities beyond the classroom: Teletandem exchanges, Zoom conversations with writers and artists, commercial conversation platforms, and AI conversation partners. These exchanges can open up forms of communication and cultural contact that are difficult to create in a traditional classroom, especially for students who may not have access to study abroad or regular interaction with speakers from other linguistic and cultural contexts. At the same time, these tools raise important questions. What kinds of communities do these exchanges create? What changes when conversation becomes mediated through platforms or AI? How do students respond to the differences between speaking with another person and interacting with an AI system designed to simulate one? What happens when intercultural exchange becomes something organized and mediated by commercial companies, especially when those relationships may at times raise questions about inequality or exploitation? The session is especially interested in presentations grounded in classroom experience, as well as broader reflections on the pedagogical and theoretical questions raised by these forms of virtual and AI-mediated exchange. Possible topics include current and emerging forms of virtual exchange, AI-mediated interaction, commercial platforms, the changing relationship between human and technological forms of communication, and the pedagogical, cultural, and ethical questions these developments may raise in the years ahead. DESCRIPTION: This session explores the growing role of virtual exchanges, commercial platforms, and AI-mediated interaction in language, literature, and culture courses. items.fullDescription: "Did I request thee, Maker?": Contemporary Cyborgs and Androids and Their Pre-Modern Antecedents Contemporary speculative fiction is saturated with androids, cyborgs, artificial intelligences, and technologically engineered forms of sentience. Yet the fantasy of constructed or quasi-human life long predates modern computing and robotics. Classical and pre-modern literature repeatedly imagines artificial beings, animated matter, virtual persons, mechanical servants, enchanted automata, and forms of life that blur the boundary between the human and the non-human. This panel invites papers that place contemporary representations of manufactured or technologically mediated beings in dialogue with their classical or pre-modern antecedents. Possible pairings might include science fiction, film, television, comics, anime, or video games alongside texts from antiquity through the early modern period. What conceptual, philosophical, theological, or aesthetic frameworks for artificial life emerge in pre-modern literature? How do earlier traditions of animation, embodiment, enchantment, or mechanical simulation anticipate contemporary debates surrounding AI, consciousness, labor, gender, race, affect, or personhood? While Frankenstein remains a central touchstone for discussions of artificial life-and itself invokes Paradise Lost as part of that genealogy-this panel is especially interested in less frequently discussed genealogies and archives. What ancestors to the android or cyborg might be found in Ovid's Metamorphoses, the works of Shakespeare, medieval romance, alchemical traditions, Jewish mysticism, Islamic philosophy, Buddhist narrative traditions, or other non-Western pre-modern texts? Possible topics may include automata and animated objects; artificial or manufactured bodies; alchemy, magic, and technological imagination; pre-modern theories of mind, soul, and consciousness; race, gender, and constructed embodiment; virtuality, simulation, and illusion; labor and mechanical life; monstrosity and the posthuman; game studies and worldbuilding; and theological or philosophical anxieties surrounding creation itself.

items.fullDescription: The 1995 film Smoke, directed by Wayne Wang, features characters who band together by frequenting a corner cigar store in Brooklyn. Paul Auster, who wrote the screenplay, once described the community his characters created as a "little universe for themselves that is not determined by blood or the past." Members of traditional, fixed communities often belong because of generational roots and longtime residency. This panel session will explore smaller, and often more liminal, communities that are forged through other means. In such communities, membership is not dependent on family ties or connection to place. This community is one of commonality: members come together through common needs, interests, traumas, or goals. They may be temporary or long lasting, healthy or dysfunctional, organized or informal. Questions to consider might include, but are not limited to, the following: Under what circumstances do these "little universe" communities form, and what is their function? How do they fit (or not fit) into the larger community, and how do they reflect or perhaps indict the larger community? How do they transform the lives of their members? What unexpected effects do the groups have on their members? What happens when these communities disband? Possible examples of these communities: Support groups Virtual communities Groups that form in institutions (colleges, prisons) Clubs and groups of people with similar interests (book clubs, game-playing clubs, hiking groups, knitting circles, etc.) Communities formed of exclusion/communities of outsiders This panel welcomes papers that examine prose fiction, poetry, film, documentary, nonfiction, and culture. items.fullDescription: Maybe no one has ever looked at a pile of papers with unbridled joy, but in a time of university-subsidized LLMs, instructors are more likely view a stack of papers with a mix of dread and horror. How many made up quotations will I have to check? How many fake citations? How many versions of "it's not ___, it's ___" can I read before my soul leaves my body? To teach writing now is to be reminded too forcefully of the critique of writing that Plato relays in the Phaedrus: "it is no true wisdom that you offer your disciples, but only its semblance, for by telling them of many things without teaching them you will make them seem to know much, while for the most part they know nothing, and as men filled, not with wisdom but with the conceit of wisdom, they will be a burden to their fellows." Plato captures here complaints that writing teachers pestered by LLM-extruded prose should recognize immediately. Many writing teachers have responded to the creation of the semblance of wisdom and its corrosive production of conceit by turning to the solution offered in Plato: the voice. This roundtable invites participants who have shifted their pedagogy to center discussion, dialogue, oral presentation, and other forms of embodied communication in response to the depredations of LLMs in higher education. How has this use of voice affected how students write and how we think about their writing? Submit abstracts of 250 words by September 30, 2026. items.fullDescription: As more and more women's stereotypical images are distributed via digital networks, active counter-activism via digital networks is an urgent need in a post-truth media environment. In the age of audio-visual curation, the cultural narrative has been traditionally controlled by state and corporate power, while today, opaque automated content moderation, algorithmic sorting and filtering, and platform capitalism of transnational streaming networks dominate the scene. The digital battlefield is a place where the feminist media studies and digital humanities converge, enabling women scholars, journalists and policy makers to work together on topics of gender equity, governance and social change. Podcasting and internet long-form discussions are important avenues for feminist knowledge production without the conventional gatekeepers, and can affect policy change, as the knowledge is directly reaching the public. These voices, however, have to constantly maneuver through algorithmic echo chambers and corporate platform architectures that have the potential to re-systemicize erasures. In this, interdisciplinary, global papers enter the scene, wading through the areas of media history, digital humanities and visual culture. These digital audio-visual environments, like those of NeMLA 2027's theme "Empowering Communities", respond to these landscapes and are the site of acts of digital sovereignty and agency by global creators and subaltern communities. Exploring the global shift from centralized media broadcasting to automated algorithmic governance, this panel analyzes how contemporary podcasts and digital audio-visual ecosystems serve as critical counter-spaces for gendered activism and subaltern expression. It welcomes interdisciplinary contributions that examine how scholars, creators, and communities collaborate to navigate algorithmic architectures, challenge systemic stereotypes, and assert digital sovereignty. items.fullDescription: I want to be accepted by society…live in a world I don't have to hide in…make choices without being in constant fear of them destroying me or the ones I care about." (Ada, liberated TanakX5 robot, on her hopes and dreams. Alex + Ada, Book 11) Many contemporary and recent speculative fiction texts interrogate the questions of "making kin" with companion species, including the companions humans might engineer and build to keep us company. In her Staying with the Trouble, Donna Haraway proposes reknitting the current order to address Capitalocene-generated problems of overpopulation and overconsumption. To survive, humans must extend their care and loyalty to other inhabitants of our shared planet, and co-construct knowledge -sympoeisis-with them. Haraway includes part-biological cyborgs in the potential so-called symbionts with whom humans should co-exist, but does not expressly include fully non-biologic, mechanical partners in her analysis. Yet, as part of the thought experiment enacted by speculative fictions of manufactured fellow beings, Haraway's prescription might be expanded to encompass sentient partners whom humans engineer and manufacture to keep themselves company. This roundtable invites papers interrogating speculative fiction solutions for expanding kinship relations to sentient non-biologic companions, whether embodied robots, virtual companions, or other. In other words, how does a particular creator of an imagined world envision expanding Haraway's Chthulucene era of "oddkin" to included fully artificial as well as natural companion species? And how do these artificial companions fare, that is, are the humans in their worlds able to embrace their right to equal standing and accord them rights?

items.fullDescription: Victor Hugo, Alexandre Dumas (father as well as son), William Wordsworth, Percy B. Shelley, Friedrich Hölderlin, G.W.F. Hegel… The list of writers from the era conventionally identified as "Romantic" to have become enthusiastic about the French Revolution could keep on going indefinitely. In fact, ever since the outbreak of the American Revolution in 1765, through the French and the Haitian Revolutions throughout the 1790's, all the way to 1848, the year that de-politicized Charles Baudelaire (according to his letter from May 5, 1852 to Narcisse Ancelle), literary production seems to have been inseparable from the process of building after and thinking social revolution. And that's because both Romanticism and the bourgeois upheavals of the late 18th century inherit and put to practice the Enlightened commitment to "the free, independent use of all of our predispositions and powers in thought and action," as Johann Adam Bergk put it in his 1795 article "Does Enlightenment Cause Revolutions?" But not every instance of Romanticism is revolutionary in the same way or engages with the big revolutions equally. And that's what makes the relationship so seminal. This panel invites papers that examine the relationships between literature, literary life, textual practice more broadly, and the social changes that occurred throughout the world from the mid 18th to the mid 19th century, from whichever angle and framework. While primarily focused on the influence these revolutions had on German, French, and English thought, we welcome papers dealing with other intellectual and social contexts, for as long as a clear connection between a literature that can be deemed "Romantic" and social revolutions is being drawn. Scholars from all over the world are invited. "Romanticism and Revolution" is a hybrid panel. Your presentation can be made in person or through Zoom. You are welcome to present remotely, although you can definitely take more advantage of the conference if you are there in person! This panel invites papers that discuss the relationships between literary production and revolution from the second half of the 18th century until the middle of the 19th. The discussion proposed by the paper can take any approach the author(s) find proper. While primarily focused on authors from the French, German, and English traditions, the panel welcomes papers discussing other contexts, for as long as the link between "Romanticism and Revolution" is somehow maintained. items.fullDescription: This panel examines how literary and cultural texts from diverse global traditions imagine masculinity not merely as an individual identity but as a relational and communal practice. In an era marked by migration, political polarization, social fragmentation, environmental crisis, and renewed struggles for collective empowerment, narratives of masculinity have become central sites through which communities negotiate belonging, responsibility, vulnerability, and resistance. While dominant models of masculinity have often been associated with hierarchy, authority, nationalism, and exclusion, contemporary world literatures increasingly depict alternative masculinities grounded in care, ethical responsibility, emotional openness, solidarity, and collective survival. Such representations challenge inherited structures of power while opening new possibilities for community formation and social transformation. This panel invites comparative and transnational approaches that explore how literary texts, films, cultural narratives, and other expressive forms construct, critique, or reimagine masculinities within local and global communities. items.fullDescription: If you've taught older literature recently, you've probably heard students ask the question "Why am I reading this?" They've got a point. Why should we read Shakespeare's plays, or Paradise Lost , or (god-forbid) "The Rape of the Lock"? We might be able to coax students into reading a Jane Austen novel or even Huckleberry Finn because they are still part of our cultural imagination, but it's less easy to coax students into reading Beowulf or Tom Jones -texts that are less familiar in form and content. As we jettison the canon and the timeless truths of literature, what do we expect reading older texts will give our students that they wouldn't otherwise understand? How do we explain our reasoning to students about why they should read texts from earlier literary periods? How do we present these earlier periods (or periodization) and their culture and ideas as relevant to our undergraduate students in our English, writing, or humanities programs? Or is relevance the problem? How might we redefine older literature in our classes, or what we (can) do with these texts? I'm particularly interested in position papers that take into consideration practical pedagogical and theoretical concerns: arguments about curricula, course development or assignments that do different things with this literature. Papers are welcome on any kind of literature/texts or periods prior to 1800.

items.fullDescription: Collective Selves: Rethinking Autobiography Beyond the Individual. Philippe Lejeune's influential formulation of the autobiographical pact has long shaped autobiography studies. The pact presumes an aligned author, narrator, and protagonist, and simultaneously privileges the singular, first-person life narrative as the normative autobiographical form. However, several personal narratives resist these assumptions. Edited autobiographies, oral histories, collaborative memoirs, and interview-based narratives often construct an autobiographical "I"/protagonist that is multiple rather than singular and that emerges across the voices of individuals whose experiences collectively narrate a shared history. Likewise, some collective life narratives depart from conventional autobiography structures, appearing as fragmented accounts, interwoven testimonies, or dispersed chapters within larger texts. This panel invites papers that examine forms of self-representation that foreground the collective. Particularly of interest are papers that interrogate the presumed unity of author, narrator, and protagonist; reconsider the autobiographical pact in light of collaborative and collective forms of narration; and explore how communities write themselves into history through shared acts of remembrance, testimony, and self-representation. Topics to consider include, but are not limited to: Collaborative and edited autobiographies Oral histories and interview-based life narratives Community and collective testimony Indigenous, Black, and diasporic collective life writing Gender, Sexuality and self testaments Archives, memory, and community self-representation Theoretical reconsiderations of the autobiographical pact and authorial voice Experimental and hybrid forms of autobiography Collective authorship, voice, and narrative authority Life writing, activism, and community formation. By centering collective modes of self-account, this panel seeks to expand the boundaries of autobiography studies and establish interventions that consider how communities, rather than individuals alone, become autobiographical subjects.

These challenges are intensified at specialized universities, meaning institutions oriented toward fields such as STEM, health sciences, business, etc., where Humanities courses are often kept to general education requirements and could be perceived as peripheral to students' professional training. By sharing concrete strategies, institutional experiences, and models of interdisciplinary partnership, this discussion aims to highlight adaptable approaches for maintaining the visibility and importance of the Humanities in specialized settings. Ultimately, the roundtable seeks to reassert the Humanities as essential to professional education. items.fullDescription: In the United States, our lives are marked by an abundance of convenience. From fresh produce year-round to two-day shipping, convenient choices feel soft, easy, and frictionless, as they have specifically been engineered to feel. Until relatively recently, it has been possible to maintain a cultural and systemic sense of alienation that makes the cost of our convenience invisible to us-to localize all of the necessary precarity and exploitation for convenience "somewhere else," (often in the Global South) and then to ignore it. However, the veil is lifting, and "somewhere else" has reached us directly--worker and labor exploitation, droughts and systemic extermination of wild animals, widening class gaps, heat waves, short and snowless winters, floods, wildfires, unprecedented weather patterns, booming microbe populations that alter the very soil we stand on. A sustainable future must be an inconvenient one, and perhaps a precarious one, unless we can remake communities with a focus on outmoded forms of convenience: reciprocity, mutual aid, de-suburbanization, and anti-capitalism. In this panel, we hope to facilitate a conversation about art, in/convenience, precarity, and resistance in community. We also hope to consider alternate views of in/convenience: What can we do to create communities in which the inconvenience of slowness is celebrated rather than derided? How can we utilize writing to grieve futures that didn't materialize? How might we create work that celebrates the pleasure of systemic and interpersonal inconvenience? How can we build resilience to inconvenience and precarity at once, together? In the tradition of scholars and writers like Lauren Berlant, Hanif Abdurraqib, Anna Lowenhaupt Tsing, and Margaret Price, how can we embrace the inconvenient as a site of connection and resistance? We welcome writers of creative nonfiction, poetry, fiction, art pieces, and hybrid works who seek to consider community and in/convenience. We are looking for writing about all forms of convenience and inconvenience, from the granular to the esoteric. After panelists share their work, the chairs will facilitate a conversation between writers and audience members.

Convention Site: Salve Regina University. Session Abtract The guiding thread of this panel develops around a curious remark by Jacques Rancière that would seem to amend a classically Aristotelian thesis: "man is a political animal because he is a literary animal," the fundamental condition of which is the "excess of words" constitutive of the human animal's politicalness. Literature (or poetry) has long been placed in close proximity to politics, as we find in Plato's Republic, where philosophy and literature-and, more generally, philosophy and politics-turn out to be perennial adversaries. That matters of literature bear upon the question of politics has featured in continental French thought for quite some time, considered in terms of the milieu of différance and event in Jacques Derrida; le partage du sensible and dissensus in Jacques Rancière; and the unpresentable and testimony to le différend in Jean-François Lyotard, among others. More recently, Geoffrey Bennington has taken up the question of the unreadable as that condition that keeps reading open to the event of alterity. What is at stake, then, in the complex relationship between literature and politics? How does literature bear witness to, or otherwise reconfigure, who counts as a speaking being, what is recognized as speech, and/or what falls out of discursive legibility as mere noise, excess, or silence? And how might mis-reading, mis-translation, and mis-understanding contribute to the politics of literature? This panel invites reflection on the figures, scenes, and events of textuality that respond to these and related questions. All critical approaches are welcome for this in-person panel. Eric J. Adamo McMaster University Hamilton, Ontario, Canada.

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers NeMLA's 58th Annual Convention - "Empowering Communities" March 6-9, 2027 | Salve Regina University, Newport, Rhode Island (Hybrid Conference) Panel Title: Tracing Female Body, Art & Economy in the Global South Primary Area / Secondary Area: Women's and Gender Studies / Interdisciplinary Humanities Modality: Hybrid Chair: Maryam Raza (University of Auckland, New Zealand) This panel explores how the historical treatment of female bodies in the Global South through the patriarchal structures of subjectification, commodification, sexualization and objectification has been reversed by contemporary strategies of resistance and reclamation. The panel examines how the postmodern woman in diverse socio-economic contexts "trains" the masculine gaze (Dixit 2024) over her body, renegotiating agency. Women increasingly reconfigure the female body through carnivalesque, alternative spaces of identity, creativity and skill through embodied forms. The female body evolves from a passive object of desire into an active, expressive, and economically productive site. items.fullDescription: This panel invites papers that examine the agency of marginalized characters in literary, visual, audiovisual, and artistic productions from the French?speaking world across any historical period. Artistic works offer numerous examples of figures who maintain an ambivalent relationship to their communities. Because of their social or ethnic origins, their divergent perspectives, or their transgression of established norms, certain characters find themselves pushed to the margins of social, familial, or professional groups. While such exclusion may appear to weaken those who experience it, this panel asks whether marginalization might also function as a source of strength. Can marginality become a generative position? Do marginalized individuals succeed in forming new communities that enable them to confront stigma and ultimately overcome it? This discussion seeks to shift our understanding of the place occupied by marginalized individuals and groups in fictional narratives. By considering the networks of solidarity that emerge among marginalized subjects, the panel explores what lies beneath their presumed inferiority, inviting critical attention to what is hidden, erased, or rendered invisible within dominant narratives. More importantly, we will examine how marginalized communities may become empowering spaces of resistance, mutual support, and hope. Drawing on approaches from cultural studies, postcolonial theory, sociolinguistics, and intersectionality, this session seeks to understand how literary, visual, audiovisual, and artistic narratives stage the tensions between marginality and belonging, strength and vulnerability. Proposals engaging with environmental humanities, posthumanism, Indigenous studies, as well as diaspora and migration studies are strongly encouraged. We also welcome submissions drawing on gender and queer studies, memory and trauma studies, digital humanities, or other interdisciplinary frameworks within the humanities. items.fullDescription: Today's ecological problems demand not only ecological awareness but also a fundamental rethinking of the human-nature relationship with the more-than-human world. Increased climatic change, species extinction, ecological degradation, and planetary instability. Challenge anthropocentric assumptions where humans are seen as separate from, superior to, or sole interpreters of nature. This panel invites papers that explore how literature, storytelling, environmental humanities, and creative pedagogies might cultivate "ecologies of attention" within teacher education and educational spaces. Rather than approaching nature as a passive object of study or a resource for human learning, the session seeks to examine how literary and cultural texts unsettle human-centered ways of knowing and open possibilities for relational, more-than-human pedagogies. How might literature invite future educators to engage with ecological interconnectedness, multispecies agency, and nonhuman forms of intelligence, communication, and temporality? What pedagogical possibilities emerge when teachers and learners encounter forests, rivers, plants, animals, weather systems, and landscapes not as background settings, but as active participants within shared ecological worlds? How can educational practices move beyond extractive or instrumental approaches to environmental learning toward forms of attentiveness, reciprocity, care, and ethical coexistence? The panel is particularly interested in pedagogical and creative engagements that explore how literary and speculative texts reshape ecological imagination and challenge anthropocentric assumptions within teacher education, curriculum studies, literacy practices, and environmental pedagogy. items.title: Against Agency - NEMLA Roundtable
items.excerpt: Over the last three decades, the humanities and social sciences have virtuously signaled their moral superiority with the empty utterance of words such as agency and resistance. items.fullDescription: Over the last three decades, the humanities and social sciences have virtuously signaled their moral superiority with the empty utterance of words such as agency and resistance. The professional managerial class, in Catherine Liu's apt analysis, "reworks political struggles for policy change and redistribution into individual passion plays, focusing its efforts on individual acts of 'giving back' or reified forms of self-transformation." In our current moment of passive horror, instead of discursively gesturing toward idealist (and condescending) notions of "empowerment," shouldn't we critically map the precise landscape of those constraints that foreclose agency and limit the ability to collectively determine social futures? Critical theorists (e.g., Adorno, Althusser, Liu, Marcuse) and historians (e.g., Johnson, Krylova, Moss) have posed a series of challenging questions to the transdisciplinary "turn to agency": against liberal notions of autonomous selfhood, universality, and choice, they ask us to contend with the ways in which people make history, yes, but not under conditions of their own choosing. In line with this predicament, this roundtable seeks to host an interdisciplinary conversation around the contingency of agency, intended not as a metaphysical horizon, but as a complex dialectic of volition and structure. We are interested in contributions that theorize "against agency." What are the processes that limit, curtail, overdetermine, or foreclose our ability to both understand and change the world (e.g., the "pitiless constraints" of material conditions, structural interpellation, epistemological violence, social domination, and mute compulsion)? How do they find expression in cultural production and academic discourses? Moreover, as members of an increasingly apolitical, elitarian class stratum, we must seek a reckoning: for this reason, we value perspectives that courageously examine how a certain "ideology of agency" in our contemporary discourse might play an operative role in limiting our horizons of action. The roundtable will be structured around two parts: each participant should be prepared to give an eight-minute spoken intervention, and then space will be opened up for informal, critical conversation. Please submit a 200-300 word abstract by 9/30 here: https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22448

items.fullDescription: This session explores how women's bodies function as contested archives of trauma, sites of testimony that dominant social, legal and political structures have often silenced or delegitimised. Drawing on feminist trauma theory, postcolonial critique and affect studies, it examines bodily memory as a form of somatic knowledge that exceeds conventional language and probes the tension between trauma's structural unspeakability and the ethical urgency of testimony and witnessing. The session invites work attentive to how race, caste, class, sexuality, coloniality and disability shape whose pain is heard and whose is erased. Relevant material includes autobiographical writing, testimonial literature, oral histories, visual and performance culture and collective protest/memorial practices with particular interest in South Asian Partition narratives and women's life writing as archives of embodied suffering and resistance. Theoretically grounded in scholars such as Judith Herman, Sara Ahmed, Veena Das, Shoshana Felman, Urvashi Butalia, Kamla Bhasin, Krishna Menon, and Dori Laub, the session also welcomes non-Western and vernacular frameworks that challenge Eurocentric trauma paradigms. Papers connecting individual testimony to systemic gendered violence, and theorising survival and creative expression as political resistance, are especially encouraged. The session calls for a feminist ethics of listening that honors women's embodied experience across geographies, resists pathologising traumatic memory and recognises speech from a wounded body as an act of defiance. Submissions: 250-300 word abstracts with a brief bio, from literary studies, history, sociology, gender studies, postcolonial studies, cultural studies, Dalit studies and allied fields. Modality: Hybrid- The session will be held in-person but a few remote presentations may be included.

items.fullDescription: Palestine and the Challenge to German Studies Northeast Modern Language Association (NeMLA) annual convention Newport, Rhode Island March 6-9, 2027 Submission Deadline: 30 September 2026 through the NeMLA portal: https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22528 Recent work in and around German Studies (Younes and Al-Taher; El Bulbeisi; Özyürek; Moses; Salehi) argues that the erasure of Palestinian identity in Germany is tied to deeper national tensions: How the country remembers its past, how it talks or avoids talking about race, what kinds of political speech are treated as acceptable, and how it confronts histories of imperialism and genocide. Moreover, scholars (Thompson and Tuzcu; Ragab; Daher) have documented how major institutions in Germany have been engaged in a wave of repression of ethnic minority communities, targeting Palestinians, other people of color, and Jewish anti-Zionists. This scholarship demonstrates how such pressures influence which voices, histories, and political positions are treated as legitimate within the field of German Studies, and which ones are marginalized. This panel invites contributions that explore how German Studies has begun or has struggled to engage with the significance of Palestine and Palestinian life, not only in contemporary German culture, politics, and literature, but within the discipline's own structures. While scholarship on Holocaust memory culture, as well as on multidirectional memory and migrant memory archives, has broadened the field's understanding of how Holocaust memory circulates and how migrant communities navigate its demands, recent work, such as articles by Catlin, Kundnani, and Rosenbrück in the New German Critique special issue "German Memory Politics at a Crossroads" (2026) provides evidence of the limits of these frameworks and the political pressures that shape them. Rather than challenge the centrality of Holocaust memory itself, this panel aims to examine how it is mobilized to foreclose other histories of violence, displacement, and coloniality, and how this foreclosing makes it difficult to integrate anti-imperialist, antiracist, and decolonial approaches that would situate Germany within broader histories of imperialism, colonial violence, and genocide. Palestine makes these dynamics visible by revealing how debates about memory shape disciplinary boundaries, how racialization and political speech determine scholarly legitimacy, and how exclusions are reproduced even within critical frameworks. This panel welcomes contributions that examine where Palestine appears, where it is actively excluded, and how these patterns expose German Studies' unresolved tensions around race, German colonial histories, and the politics of knowledge production. The goal of this panel is to open a conversation about how German Studies might expand beyond memory-centered approaches toward more globally attuned, anti?imperialist, and decolonial analytical frameworks. Topics include but are not limited to: · Intersectional decolonial feminist frameworks and praxes · Critiques of white Western imperial feminism · "Pinkwashing" and "homonationalism" to justify colonial violence and dehumanize Indigenous communities · The role of anti-Palestinian racism in mainstream anti-immigrant backlash and far-right political actors · Scapegoating of Muslims as the new Nazis in the theory of "imported anti-Semitism" (Özyürek) · Germany's colonial and neocolonial relationships to the broader region of West Asia · Integrating Palestinian perspectives into pedagogy, curriculum, and study abroad advising · Courses and lesson plans that include the Nakba and its continuity · German Studies and BDS/academic boycott · The "Historikerstreit 2.0" and attacks on "postcolonialism" · The history of East German solidarity with Palestinians · Student and faculty support in campus organizing for Palestine solidarity, and institutional and departmental barriers Abstracts: Please submit 300-word abstracts by 30 September 2026 though the NeMLA portal: https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22528 For questions, please contact the panel organizer Maria Grewe (mgrewe@jjay.cuny.edu).

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: NANO: New American Notes Online (ISSN: 2160-0104) Special Issue 18: Exploring the Boundary Waters of the Blue Humanities Special Issue Guest Editors: Eric Denbang Kunkuri and Dana Van Kooy Deadline: 16 October 2026 Publication: spring/summer 2027 Full CFP Details: https://nanocrit.com/index.php/home/cfp-plus-submissions-new The creative and scholarly work being done in the blue humanities has deepened our turn towards exploring waterways and boundary waters. The currents circulating through the blue humanities flow into and from myriad disciplines, including anthropology, biology, decolonial studies, feminist/queer studies, geography, history, indigenous studies, literature, music, performance studies, philosophy, and the visual arts. The cultural and theoretical inlets being carved out by work in the blue humanities have proven generative in terms of developing a distinctive metaphor-laden language, analytic methods like Kamau Brathwaite's theory of "tidalectics," and new ways of submerging ourselves in both historical and unprecedented questions about the water that is in and, as Rachel Carson notes in her famous title, "around us." For this special issue, we invite submissions of traditional and multimodal essays of up to 5,000 words (excluding works cited) that explore the boundary waters of the blue humanities. items.fullDescription: TRANSPOSITIONES Journal for Transdisciplinary and Intermedial Culture Studies / Zeitschrift fu?r transdisziplinäre und intermediale Kulturforschung, ISSN 2749-4128 (print), 2749-4136 (online), Vol. 6, No. 2 (2027) Call for Papers Thematic focus of the issue: Earth / Sediment / Trace: Geologies, Material Memories, and the More-than-Living World Across the environmental humanities, increasing attention has been devoted to the geological dimensions of culture and the cultural dimensions of the Earth. Geohumanities, critical mineral studies, energy humanities, environmental justice scholarship, and related fields have opened new perspectives on extraction, sedimentation, toxicity, waste, material memory, and deep time. At a moment marked by accelerating ecological transformations and growing awareness of the material infrastructures that sustain contemporary life, geological matter has emerged as a crucial site for rethinking history, memory, environment, and cultural imagination. Rather than treating the Earth as a passive backdrop to human activity, recent scholarship has approached rocks, minerals, soils, fossils, sediments, and other material formations as archives of planetary processes, environmental change, cultural memory, and political conflict. Questions of resource extraction, environmental justice, and slow violence increasingly intersect with inquiries into deep temporalities, material traces, sacred landscapes, and the long afterlives of human and more-than-human actions. This issue invites contributions that explore how literature, art, media, philosophy, religion, and cultural practices engage with geological matter, deep time, sedimented histories, and the material conditions of planetary life. We especially welcome work that investigates the cultural significance of rocks, minerals, fossils, soil, waste, ruins, and other forms of more-than-living matter, while also addressing questions of environmental justice, resource extraction, toxicity, and slow violence. We welcome analyses of literary, philosophical, historical, and cultural texts from a wide range of regions and traditions, including comparative and transnational perspectives. Topics may include: • geohumanities and geological imagination; • earth, stone, sediment, dust, and soil; • lithic ecologies and critical mineral studies; • deep time, planetary temporalities, and environmental history; • extractivism, mining, resource conflicts, and energy humanities; • environmental justice and slow violence; • toxic landscapes and contaminated environments; • waste, ruins, landfills, and material afterlives; • fossils, paleontology, and material histories of life; • material memory, archives, traces, and sedimented histories; • sacred geographies, holy mountains, stones, and pilgrimage landscapes; • archaeology, antiquarianism, and the materialities of the past; • textual strata, sedimented knowledge, and epistemic layers; • geological trauma, memory, and post-catastrophic landscapes; • petrofiction, climate fiction, and environmental storytelling; • artistic and literary engagements with earth materials; • relations between living and non-living matter; • fungi, decomposition, and processes of material transformation; • posthumanist, new materialist, and decolonial approaches to geology and the earth. A final decision regarding abstract acceptance will be made by October 31. Deadline for submitting completed manuscripts: February 28, 2027. The issue is expected to be published in the autumn of 2027.

items.fullDescription: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture, and Activism Call for Chapters Description: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture and Activism addresses the critical need for a comprehensive academic survey of Hip Hop's connection to sport as a preeminent sociological and political force among Millennials and Generation Z. This handbook maps the emerging critical terrain where Hip Hop intersects with the sports-industrial complex, digital activism, and the persistent structures of racial capitalism and white supremacy. As the culture enters its second half-century, it serves as an emergent space for self-expression and identity formation, both to hegemonic and counter-hegemonic ends. The leading objectives of this volume are to delineate how Hip Hop's relationship with sport provides narrative resources for youth to explore their social realities in the context of late-stage capitalism and its bedfellows: white supremacy and patriarchy. This handbook explores both the route and roots of Hip Hop expression through the lens of the African diaspora and the historical relationship between Black expressive history and social movements. This handbook is also interested in the ways in which Hip Hop's relationship with sport can be oriented both towards liberation and political conservatism, particularly in the context of Hip Hop's historical and presentist embrace of Donald Trump and his representative movements. This project aims to both engage Hip Hop's historical relationship with sports (professional and amateur) as well as its contemporary shifts,such as the institutionalization of breaking in the 2024 Olympics and the rise of representation activism in major sports leagues (NBA, NFL) that create new tensions between cultural authenticity and corporate appropriation. It is intended to define the current state of theory and establish a foundation for future scholarship across the interdisciplinary fields of hip-hop studies, sport management, and Africana studies. Since this project is a handbook and not an anthology, the chapter topics have already been pre-selected by the editors. However, we encourage submissions that engage the specific areas of expertise of each contributor, and the contributor is welcome to interpret the proposed topics according to their own research and experience. The targeted audience for this handbook are advanced high school students and undergraduates, so chapters should be written with this audience in mind. We invite abstract submissions from Hip Hop practitioners, sport sociologists, scholars, graduate students, postgraduate researchers, and early career researchers. Authors will be notified of their acceptance by November 30th, 2026. Full chapters of 4,000-6,000 words (including references) are due by April 30th, 2027. For further questions, contact Dr. Micah J. Dobson (mjdobson92@gmail.com ) and Dr. Tyler Bunzey (tylerbunzey@gmail.com). items.fullDescription: Diane Long Hoeveler and Tamar Heller's Approaches to Teaching Gothic Fiction: British and American Traditions (MLA Options for Teaching) was published in 2003; Anna Powell and Andrew Smith's Teaching the Gothic (Palgrave) was published in 2006. While both texts are excellent guides for teachers of the Gothic, quite a lot has happened in the twenty years since these texts appeared, not the least of which was a Gothic-infused global pandemic and the insidious rise of artificial intelligence in daily life. Academics today are and have been teaching the Gothic at a time when the world's problems - rising fascism, global conflict, climate change, the devaluation of Higher Education, among many others - make the world itself seem downright Gothic. This collection will seek to provide updated reflections, evaluations, and strategies on teaching the Gothic and utilising or creating Gothic pedagogy in the contemporary moment and beyond. Courses on or including the Gothic are taught in a wide variety of venues within and outside academia; settings include community colleges, traditional undergraduate programmes, graduate programmes, community centres, prisons and reformatories. Classrooms themselves vary greatly, from giant lecture halls to small upper-level seminars to fully online virtual spaces. Students of the Gothic come from all ages and backgrounds, and include native speakers of English and students acquiring English later in life. These contexts, venues, and audiences present different challenges for the instructor, and require unique approaches to make for successful learning experiences. We are seeking contributions from a range of scholars at different ranks and types of institutions (as well as outside of them) to present a broad understanding of the diversity of how we study and teach the Gothic today, and to provide new directions for the future. We already have interest from an academic press. Potential topics might include but are not restricted to one or a mixture of the following: Teaching the Gothic in the midst of a crisis (e.g. pandemic, war, from a distance or physically within such spaces) Teaching the Gothic outside of the university / in non-traditional settings Challenges of AI to teaching the Gothic The use of various digital platforms in teaching / student research Gothic and the archives in contemporary times What texts (and which editions) absolutely must be on any Gothic syllabus (and why)? Gothic forms (teaching beyond traditional formats, for instance) Gothic theory as pedagogy (in times of crisis particularly) Syllabus organizational strategies and rationales: Chronological? Thematic? Canon? Decolonizing the Gothic syllabus Preparing for and managing class discussions about violence, sexual violence, trauma, discrimination, or other tough topics that arise in the Gothic? Strategies for teaching a Gothic course for an audience unfamiliar with the Gothic / unfamiliar with academia / non-traditional students. Gothic and public engagement / school outreach Opportunities for service learning / personal and professional development in the Gothic course Creative forms of assessment in the Gothic classroom Neurodivergence and the Gothic Designing assignments with AI in mind Cancel culture and the Gothic Co-editors Bridget Marshall (University of Massachusetts, Lowell) and Jen Baker (University of Warwick, UK) seek abstracts of 300-500 words for chapters which will demonstrate innovative approaches to teaching the Gothic or engaging with or creating new Gothic pedagogies, particularly situated within recent contexts. We are open to a variety of forms, including case studies, reflective essays, theoretically informed essays, and other formats that can best showcase pedagogical insights. If your proposed essay includes samples of work by students/participants we will require written permissions before publication. Please also include a brief professional bio of 300 words (max) with your abstract. Please send your abstract and bio by 10 November 2026 to Bridget_Marshall@uml.edu and J.Baker.5@warwick.ac.uk We are happy to answer questions at the same address.

items.fullDescription: Journal of Studies in Language, Culture and Society (JSLCS) ISSN / E-ISSN: 2716-9189 / 2676-1750 Publisher: University of Bejaia Editor-in-chief: Prof. Nadia Idri, Author Guidelines for JSLCS Standards Our Goal: To be a leading international, multidisciplinary forum for high-quality research. To achieve this, we require your active partnership in building a rigorous, visible, and influential scholarly community. 1. Core Philosophy: Quality, Originality, and International Contribution To be considered, your manuscript must make a clear, original, and significant contribution to its field on an international level. We prioritize research that engages with global scholarly conversations, not just regional or national discussions. Ask yourself: Why would a scholar on another continent find this paper important? 2. Abstract: Your International Showcase The abstract is your most critical tool for attracting an international readership. Length & Detail: Provide a structured abstract of 300-350 words. Use clear headings: Objective, Methodology, Results, Conclusion, Significance/Contribution. Content: Explicitly state the paper's novelty and its significance to the international research community. Avoid generic statements. Specify the gap you fill and how your findings advance the field globally. Language: Must be in excellent, native-level English. Consider professional editing if needed. This is non-negotiable for discoverability. 3. Manuscript Scope & "The Identity Challenge" JSLCS is multidisciplinary, but your paper must have a sharp, focused identity. Connect to Core Themes: While we cover language, culture, and society, your manuscript must clearly fit within one or two defined sub-fields. Justify Broad Relevance: If your topic is regionally specific (e.g., a case study in Algeria), the Introduction and Conclusion must explicitly articulate its theoretical, methodological, or comparative implications for international research. Avoid being "a paper of everything": We will desk-reject manuscripts that are overly broad, lack a clear theoretical framework, or do not connect to specific scholarly debates. 4. References & Engagement with the Global Scholarly Community Your reference list is a map of your scholarly engagement and is crucial for our global profile. Volume & Recency: A minimum of 25-30 high-quality references is expected. A significant majority should be from the last 5 years, demonstrating engagement with current discourse. Source Quality: Prioritize references from Scopus/Web of Science-indexed journals and reputable international academic presses (Routledge, Springer, Palgrave, John Benjamins, etc.). International Dialogue: Your literature review must engage with key international scholars and seminal works in your field, not just literature from a single region. Style: Strict adherence to APA 7th Edition. 5. Authorship & Affiliation International Collaboration: Research conducted by international teams or comparing multiple contexts is highly encouraged. Institutional Email & ORCID: All corresponding authors must provide an institutional email address and a valid ORCID ID. This is mandatory for submission. Author Profiles: Authors are encouraged to maintain active, public scholarly profiles (e.g., Google Scholar, Scopus Author ID, institutional webpage). 6. Language and Accessibility for an International Audience The full manuscript must be submitted in English. To enhance accessibility, we recommend that authors of highly regionally-focused studies consider including an extended summary (500-600 words) in the article's appendix, detailing the context and international relevance for non-specialists. 7. Ethical Rigor & Transparency AI Use Disclosure: Any use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools in the writing, editing, or analysis process must be transparently declared in the methodology or acknowledgments section. Describe the tool used and its purpose. AI cannot be listed as an author. Plagiarism Check: All submissions will be screened. Similarity must be below 20% (excluding references). Ethical Compliance: Studies involving humans must include proof of ethics approval. Submission Checklist: Before submitting via ASJP, ensure your manuscript: Makes a clear international contribution. Has a detailed, structured abstract highlighting novelty and significance. Fits a defined niche within our broad scope. Contains 25-30+ references (can be more), mostly recent and from high-indexed sources. Engages with international literature. Is written in excellent, polished English. Uses the correct template and APA 7th style. Includes author ORCID iD and institutional email. Has a declaration on AI use (if applicable).
