items.fullDescription: The Southern Humanities Conference, 2027 Call for Papers Conference Theme: Divergence, Convergence, Emergence Knoxville, TN, January 28-31, 2027 The Southern Humanities Conference offers an opportunity for scholars, artists, writers, musicians, performers, and humanists of all kinds to share their knowledge, research, work, and experiences in an interdisciplinary, welcoming, and engaging intellectual space. For 2027 our conference theme will be "Divergence, Convergence, Emergence." Divergent thinking is a hallmark of creative endeavors ranging from the visual and performative arts to scientific inquiry. It can also signify a transgression of a custom or standard, or even a social more or behavioral norm, through contravention or subversion of what others consider "ordinary" or "natural." On the other hand, the benefits of group diversity are undeniably numerous and valuable in education, collaboration, and problem-solving. Convergent thinking can help triangulate resolutions to mysteries in historical systems and literary plot structures, among other questions. Convergence can also be considered a precursor to meaningful communal and cooperative social and cultural interactions. The notion of emergence-a phenomenon in which novel, unpredictable, and sometimes unexpected outcomes arise from a constellation of interactions between simpler underlying elements-provides a way of understanding origins and evolutions of phenomena that interest the analytical and imaginative mind. Emergence is also often associated with the concept of synthesis and the idea that the whole can be greater than the sum of its parts. The intersections of (and interstices between) emergence, divergence, and convergence serve as the stimulus for our collective conversation in Knoxville and offers us a platform for appraising the world around us. The Southern Humanities Conference invites proposals for papers on any aspect of the theme "Divergence, Convergence, Emergence" broadly conceived. Our conference themes are meant to be inspiring and prompt reflection, not limiting. The topic is interdisciplinary and invites proposals from all areas of study, as well as creative pieces including but not limited to performance, music, art, and literature. Customary paper and full panel proposals are invited, as are ones for creative presentation formats like roundtables and demonstrations. Moreover, the Southern Humanities Conference welcomes proposals from teachers and professionals outside the academy, as well as from scholars in the early stages of their academic careers. Please note that the name of our organization simply reflects its having been founded in the U.S. South; no presenter is expected to present anything "southern," though southern topics are also welcomed. Conference attendees come from all over the United States, Canada, and overseas. items.fullDescription: Working Title: Girlboss and Puzzle-Boy: Gender in the Comic Detective TV Genre Series: DeGruyter Brill book series, Pop Culture in Context, series editors Liz Faber, Emily Hamilton-Honey & Judith Rauscher! Editor: Dr. Marc A. Ouellette, Old Dominion University (mouellet@odu.edu) Project Overview and Rationale We often think of the police procedural as a very serious genre with rigid constraints, particularly in terms of gender, heroism, morality, character types, "pulled from the headlines" stories, and a heavy dose of forensic evidence. This edited collection, critically examines the rise of the comic variant of the detective genre and with it, the revision of the gender order in terms of physicality, puzzle-solving, and the emotional labor required to support the star. The more recent development of the hybrid comic-detective show, from the long-running Death in Paradise and The Brokenwood Mysteries, The Miss Fisher Mysteries, to newer breakout hits like Deadloch, Professor T, The Chelsea Detective, Death Valley, and Ludwig, makes several important interventions, making the genre a riddle and puzzle-based "whodunnit." In this edited collection, we seek to examine what makes this genre an international and cross-cultural phenomenon. In particular, these shows and similar offerings from competitors, refigure the detective from being deceivingly and deliberately inept as a manipulative ploy into an actually bumbling, frequently helpless, and always awkward figure who routinely needs saving and protection, especially from women who perform more heroic roles in addition to their own detective skills. Of further interest is the fact that many of these productions are popular in countries other than the one(s) in which they are set, and others (Miss Fisher and Professor T) are adaptations, and all are available on local and streaming services. Thus, we welcome proposals addressing a wide array of topics across media, genre, and nationalities. The book welcomes scholars from interdisciplinary fields, including media and popular culture, gender studies, television studies, cultural studies, and genre studies, to contribute to a study of the evolution of the television detective genre in a post-Sherlock Holmes, post-CSI, post-truth era, where the focus has shifted from the detective's profound heroism to a relatable, if frustrating, human fallibility. Moving beyond the traditional heroic masculinity of earlier police procedurals, this collection argues that this new detective figure is not a profound hero, but rather a savant whose primary skill is a highly specialized form of diagnostic logic and pattern recognition. His surrounding female colleagues-often a single female superior, a team of women, or a female romantic lead-serve as his emotional and social interpreters, managing his relationships, smoothing over his eccentricities, and providing the patient, holistic perspective that he lacks. This dynamic reconfigures the procedural form, creating a hybrid genre that marries the intricate plotting of the police procedural with the interpersonal humor of a character-driven comedy. Graduate students and emerging researchers are especially welcome in this process! Topics might include, but are not limited to · Reflections of contemporary anxieties about gender, social competence, and labor. · Individual case studies of series or episodes (including but not limited to those listed above) · American exceptionalism, responses, and adaptations · Space and place in the genre, including the small town or neighborhood trope · Literary Adaptation and/or cross-cultural adaptation · Defining the comic-detective genre · Comparative considerations of The Residence (and others) among the genre · Historical patterns in the genre · Gender performances and gender tropes · Heroism, femininities, and the role of wise women · Fragile, anxious masculinities and the "prestige male" · The quirky best friend (or relative) trope · Racial diversity (or lack thereof) among main characters · Puzzles, games, riddles and the genre · The therapeutic aspects of solving the case · Heteronormativity and/or queer romance · Celebrity casting and fan studies · Social blindspots and the value of the team · Nostalgia and tradition · From deductive hero to puzzle-solving Sisyphus and the post-heroic detective · the regional and cultural variations of the awkward detective archetype. · the aesthetics of awkwardness and formal analysis of camera work, editing, and sound design to create comedic moments from social gaffes. We invite scholars from multiple disciplines to submit abstracts (300-500 words) by 1 Dec. 2026, with completed papers due 31 May 2027. Please send abstracts and inquiries to mouellet@odu.

items.fullDescription: The International Journal of English Literature, Social Sciences, and Multidisciplinary Studies (IJELS) publishes original research papers, review articles, and case studies that advance scholarly knowledge across English literature, social sciences, and multidisciplinary studies. The journal provides a global platform for researchers, educators, and professionals to share innovative ideas, critical analyses, and interdisciplinary perspectives. Submission open to Current Issue Feedback Notification: within 1 Month after submission (Online Peer Review System) IJELS welcomes high-quality submissions on a broad range of topics, including but not limited to: English Literature and Language Studies - English literature, world literature, comparative literature, interdisciplinary approaches to literature, literature and media, critical theory, English language teaching and learning, communicative language teaching (CLT), task-based language teaching (TBLT), second language acquisition, English language testing and assessment, syllabus design and curriculum development, applied linguistics, corpus linguistics, discourse analysis, translation studies, English globalization, and English-speaking cultures. Social Sciences and Humanities - Anthropology, Sociology, Psychology, Political Science, Economics, Education, Geography, History, Law, International Relations, Criminology, Public Administration, Development Studies, Human Rights, Social Welfare, Gender Studies, and Ethics. Arts and Cultural Studies - Performing Arts (music, theatre, and dance), Visual Arts, Cultural and Cross-Cultural Studies, Media Studies, Communication Studies, and Philosophy. Business, Law, and Information Studies - Business Studies, Corporate Governance, Industrial Relations, Information Science, Library Science, and Paralegal Studies. Multidisciplinary Studies - Research that bridges multiple academic disciplines to address complex social, cultural, linguistic, educational, technological, or global challenges. IJELS particularly values cross-cutting studies that integrate methodologies and perspectives from different fields to generate new insights and foster innovation. IJELS encourages diverse theoretical, empirical, and methodological approaches that promote intellectual exchange and interdisciplinary collaboration, fostering research at the dynamic intersection of literature, language, social sciences, and multidisciplinary inquiry. You may submit your article to: ijels.infogain@gmail.com

items.fullDescription: Editors: Dana Lee Baker and Matthew Mendez Garcia Publisher: Edward Elger Publishing Submission deadline for abstracts: 1 January 2027 We invite proposals for entries in an edited academic handbook on the politics of neurodiversity. This volume will bring together interdisciplinary perspectives on neurodiversity as a political, cultural, institutional, legal, and epistemic phenomenon. The handbook seeks to advance critical scholarship on how neurodivergence is governed, represented, contested, institutionalized, commodified, resisted, and politicized across local, national, and global contexts. We welcome contributions from scholars across the humanities and social sciences, as well as practitioner-scholars, activists, and community-based researchers. We are especially interested in contributions that situate neurodiversity within broader debates concerning disability politics, citizenship, identity, labor, education, race, gender, capitalism, biopolitics, medicalization, technology, and social movements. The handbook aims to foster dialogue across disciplines and perspectives. We particularly encourage submissions from: Neurodivergent scholars Early-career researchers Disabled and scholar-activist contributors Contributors outside North America and Western Europe Interdisciplinary and collaborative teams We welcome theoretical, empirical, historical, normative, and methodological approaches. Example Topics Include (but are not limited to) · Neurodiversity & Progressivism · Neurodiversity & Liberalism · Neurodiversity & Socialism · Neurodiversity & Conservatism · Extremism, hate, and neurodiversity · Feminist neuroinclusion · Neurodiversity & class power · Neurodiversity, Faith, and Politics · Political Histories of Neurodiversity in Nations other than the United States · Neurodiversity and the politics of aging · Profiles of specific activist/advocacy groups · Black neurodivergence · Neurodiversity in International Politics · Positive Rights to Neuroinclusion · Neurodiversity, Gender, and Sexuality · Neurodiversity and Public Sector Employment · Neurodiversity and Public Sector Ethics Contribution Format We envision concise, accessible, and analytically rigorous entries suitable for scholars, students, practitioners, and policymakers. Proposals should include: A title An abstract of approximately 250-500 words A brief author biography (100-150 words) Completed entries be approximately 3000 words, inclusive of bibliography and figures. Entries must meet requirements of European Accessibility Act. Entry authors must not use AI to generate text or enter their drafts into an AI system. Submission Information Please send proposals and inquiries to: dana.baker@csuci.edu Deadline for abstracts: 1 January 2027 Notification of acceptance: 15 February 2027 Draft chapters due: 15 August 2027

items.fullDescription: Public Humanities is a new international open access, cross-disciplinary, peer-reviewed journal at the intersection of humanities scholarship and public life. The journal invites proposals for themed issues that pose urgent questions on contemporary public issues that require rigorous and relevant humanities knowledge. The journal invites submissions to its upcoming Themed Issue 'The How-To Issue', which will be edited by Jeffrey R. Wilson. Deadline for submissions 1 January 2027. Description Public humanities often require an expert in one area to learn another field or skill on-the-fly or to collaborate effectively across boundaries of specialization. Especially for younger thinkers and doers, fear of the unknown combines with taken-for-granted assumptions about standard forms of humanities work to prevent our pursuit of promising public humanities projects and careers. Even veteran humanities scholars who have extensive expertise in areas vitally important to public life can crumble when confronted with the prospect of moving outside their comfort zone of academic protocols to engage with audiences via new formats or professional pathways. This issue invites practical guidance on doing public humanities. That work often involves meeting audiences where they are via media, formats, and professions that require (1) conceptual understanding of what these venues offer and (2) technical training in the nuts-and-bolts of best practices. The How-To Issue will feature a series of case studies, reflections and essays by people who have had success in a variety of formats related to public humanities (e.g., museums, activism, podcasts, policy work, etc.) offering critical reflection and guidance to people in the next generation who might be interested in those pathways but aren't really sure where to start or how to do it. From public writing to social media, from graduate program administration to empirical research, from fundraising to publishing, the issue will provide concrete case studies of successes, failures, lessons learned the hard way, and time-tested strategies for turning ideas into realities. The editor invites papers covering any form of public humanities, including but not limited to: Activism Blogs Book Clubs Community Conversations Cultural Organizations Educational Departments Empirical Studies Evaluation Funding and fundraising Grants Libraries Mass Media Multimedia Formats Museums Podcasts Policy Practice-Based Research Program Administration Public Programs and Events Public Schools (Pre-College) Public Writing Researching the Public Humanities Social Media Websites Submissions can include any or all of the follow article types: Article type? items.fullDescription: Public Humanities is an international open-access, cross-disciplinary, peer-reviewed journal at the intersection of humanities scholarship and public life. The journal invites submissions for the upcoming issue, Musical Commemorations and Contestations in Postcolonial Contexts, which will be guest edited by Bart Paul Vanspauwen, Ana-María Alarcón-Jiménez, and Livia Jiménez Sedano. Deadline for submissions: 1 February 2027 Description This special issue examines how sonic and kinetic practices-music and dance-are mobilised, contested, and governed within postcolonial commemorative and institutional contexts. It centres communities whose musical and choreographic traditions are routinely staged, suppressed, or appropriated by state institutions and heritage bureaucracies, bringing scholarship on chronically under-represented practices into a single, freely accessible comparative framework across language spheres and colonial legacies. The collection asks how music and dance function within-or in dialogue with-transnational institutions designed to consolidate language-based cultural systems, focusing on commemorative occasions and the sonic contestations they generate. From a hegemonic perspective, such commemorations produce collective memories that reproduce post-imperial geographies. From a critical perspective, they enact a persistent coloniality in which colonial-era categories endure in commemorative form. Submissions will be assessed on their engagement with one or more of the following: Musical and dance performance at official commemorative events Indigenous or colonial remembrance through music and dance Postcolonial justice and reparation via musical expression Tensions between state-sponsored and grassroots practices The instrumentalisation of intangible cultural heritage Decolonial approaches to commemoration The strongest submissions will offer a comparative or theoretically grounded account of how official institutions mediate culture through sound and movement, and what alternative practices emerge in response. Two original concepts anchor the issue: Sonic and kinetic governance: states' use of music and dance to construct authorised collective memory. Sonic and kinetic resistance: communities' use of the same media to contest that governance. The issue welcomes a diversity of perspectives and especially encourages submissions from early career researchers. It carries an explicit social mission aligned with international agendas on cultural heritage, inclusive societies, and accountable institutions, giving it purchase beyond academic audiences alone. Submission Guidelines Articles should be no more than 7,000 words, excluding the abstract, footnotes, and bibliography. Submissions should be written in accessible language for a wide readership across and beyond the humanities: see How to Write for Public Humanities. Authors should consult the journal's Author Instructions prior to submission. All authors must declare any funding and/or competing interests upon submission (see the journal's Publishing Ethics guidelines for more information). Articles will be peer reviewed for both content and style. Accepted articles will be published digitally as open access in the journal. Contacts The editor is happy to discuss potential articles: Bart Paul Vanspauwen bvanspauwen@fcsh.unl.pt Questions regarding peer review can be sent to: publichumanities@cambridge.org Submit an Article All submissions should be made through the Public Humanities online peer review system. items.fullDescription: Our conference is a global online gathering of educators, instructional designers, learning innovators, researchers, and industry leaders dedicated to shaping the future of learning. LXD has emerged as a powerful bridge between learning design and educational technology, combining pedagogical expertise with technological innovation to create engaging, learnercentred experiences. This conference provides a unique platform for sharing cutting-edge practices, innovative approaches, and emerging trends in LXD across diverse educational and professional contexts. The conference programme includes keynote presentations, interactive workshops, panel discussions, session meetings and networking opportunities. We invite contributions from the following fields: 1) Learning Experience Design Foundations; 2) Learning Sciences and Pedagogy; 3) EdTech and Digital Innovation; 4) AI and the Future of Learning; 5) User Experience and Interface Design for Learning; 6) Workplace Learning and Professional Development; 7) Inclusion, Equity, and Accessibility. PARTICIPATION Conference language is English. To participate in the conference, please fill in a registration form on our website https://ld-initiatives.ch/en/conferences/ by March 05, 2027. The confirmation of conference participation will be sent within two weeks from the submission date but not later than March 12, 2027. Conference fee: 100 CHF. For participation in the conference both speakers and listeners will be awarded with ECTS credits (1 ECTS credit for speakers and 0,5 ECTS credits for listeners), which will be stated in the certificate of attendance. Certificates of attendance will be issued to all participants, including speakers and attendees, contingent upon their physical presence at the conference. REQUIREMENTS FOR SPEAKERS Agenda: plenary speeches - 30 minutes, section speeches - 15 minutes; discussion time - 10 minutes. PUBLICATION OF ABSTRACTS All conference participants may submit abstracts for publication. Abstracts will be published in the e-Book of Abstracts containing ISBN and DOI numbers. The language of publication is English. The deadline for abstracts submission is March 05, 2027. Abstracts must be downloaded in the registration form on our website: https://ld-initiatives.ch/en/conferences/. The abstract must contain 250-300 words, excluding references. The abstract must be preceded by the name(s) of the author(s), including their title(s), affiliation, and country (all in the abovementioned order). The title of the abstract must be in bold, all capitals, centered. References, if applicable (presented in the end of the abstract), and in-text citations must conform to the APA Style. All submitted abstracts will be subjected to the double-blind peer review process. The editorial board reserves the right to decline papers that contain plagiarized content or do not conform to the norms and subject matter of the conference. ENQUIRIES For any questions concerning the conference, please contact Dr. Nataliia Gach at info@ldinitiatives.ch or by phone: +41 78 340 32 13. For more information visit our website https://ld-initiatives.ch/en/conferences/.
